instructions: Corporate product film narrator presenting to a company's management team. Calm, confident and warm, with quiet pride in the product. Mid-paced and clear, natural pauses between sentences. A slight lift of tension when something fails, relief when it recovers. Read numbers clearly. No exaggeration, no sales hype.

lines.text: Right now, two hundred and forty car park stations are running across our network.
Each one has a PC in the booth, cameras over every lane, and programs that must never stop.
This is how we keep watch over all of them.
On every station PC runs POSvc, a small Windows service.
It watches the processor, the memory and the disks; the services and the programs; every camera and lane station; the ports; and the log files, line by line.
Every thirty seconds it reports in, over two channels: one for data, and one for control.
On the server, a health sweep checks every station, every thirty seconds.
When something fails, it is flagged in about seventeen seconds, and the alert lights the bell on every screen. Telegram and email alerts can be switched on, too.
A problem has to hold for two sweeps before it alerts, so a passing flicker never wakes anyone up.
On the first of October, at CK36, both lanes went dark. Twenty-three seconds later, all four devices were flagged.
Open a station, and it draws itself, lane by lane.
Entry lanes on the left, exit lanes on the right, and the shared cameras below; each device finds its lane by its name.
Green packets mean a lane is answering. When one stops, its link breaks in red, and you can see exactly which device.
Click a camera, and its live picture opens, streamed through the server.
Click a lane station, and its screen is in front of you, with the mouse and keyboard.
The station's password stays on the server, never in the browser, and every session is recorded.
Many problems can be fixed from right here.
Ping a device. Test a port. Restart a service. Search a log.
But a station only runs commands on its own allow list. There is no open shell, and anything else is refused.
Every command is recorded: who sent it, and how it ended.
New software is signed before it leaves, with a key that never touches the server.
Each station checks the signature and the checksum, backs up what it has, and only then installs.
If anything fails, it rolls itself back.
Even the agent updates itself this way. A helper swaps in the new version, waits for it to start, and puts the old one back if it does not.
Step back, and the whole fleet becomes a galaxy.
Every station is a star on one of four arms, and a problem raises a beacon you can fly to.
Or step into a single car park, and see its lanes, its booth, and how many lots are free, live.
People sign in with their own accounts.
Four roles decide what each person can do, from viewer to super admin, and a scope decides which stations they can see.
Every sign-in, command, camera view and remote session lands in the audit report, ready to export.
ParkOps is built in-house, at Re Sustainability.
Since June: seven hundred and eighty-three changes, one hundred and ninety-eight releases, and nine hundred automated tests that check every change.
ParkOps Watch Dog. Know first.
